title: Transactions & Isolation
summary: Two people, one seat, the same millisecond. How databases keep concurrent changes correct.

goals.text: Deadlocks and constraints as a safety net
Short transactions with holds that expire

steps.title: One seat left
body: Ana and Ben both want the last seat at a concert. Their requests land on different app servers, which share one database.
The booking code looks reasonable: read how many seats are left, and if there’s one, write the booking.

callout.text: Each request on its own is correct. The trouble only appears when two run at the same time.

card.title: Book a seat
lines: n = SELECT left FROM seats WHERE id = 7
# n − 1 is worked out in the app

steps.title: Both of them get it
body: Both servers read “1 seat left” before either has written. Both decide the seat is free, both write, and both send a confirmation.
One seat, two tickets. This is a race condition — here a lost update: Ben’s write silently overwrote Ana’s.

callout.text: Races are rare in testing and common in production — exactly when it’s busiest, like the moment tickets go on sale.

steps.title: A transaction alone doesn’t stop it
body: Wrap it in BEGIN … COMMIT and the booking becomes all-or-nothing — but it can still be sold twice. Under the default isolation level of most databases (read committed), each read simply sees the latest committed value: 1.
Isolation is the part of a transaction that says what concurrent transactions can see of each other. The default is deliberately weak, for speed.

callout.text: ACID’s “I” is a dial, not a switch. Know which level your database uses by default (PostgreSQL and SQL Server: read committed; MySQL: repeatable read).

steps.title: Lock the row while you decide
body: Read with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Ana’s transaction locks row 7; when Ben’s tries to read it, the database makes him wait until Ana commits (watch his request hold at the database).
Then Ben reads the new value — 0 — and gets a polite “sold out”.

callout.text: Locks are held until COMMIT, so keep these transactions short: never wait for a user, a payment API or anything slow while holding one.

changes: + Ben waits ~40 ms for Ana’s lock

steps.title: Or do it in one statement
body: Often you don’t need to read first at all. Let the database check and change in one atomic step:
UPDATE seats SET left = left − 1 WHERE id = 7 AND left > 0 — then look at how many rows it changed. 1 means you got the seat; 0 means it was gone.

callout.text: Counters, stock levels and balances are usually safest as a single conditional UPDATE. No gap between check and change, no lock held across round trips.

changes: ~ Check and change in one UPDATE
~ Ben’s update changes 0 rows → sold out

steps.title: Optimistic: check a version number
body: Locks are pessimistic: they assume a conflict and make others wait. Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare: read the row with its version, then write … WHERE id = 7 AND version = 8, bumping it to 9.
If someone got there first, the version no longer matches, the write changes 0 rows, and you reload and try again. Nobody waits.

callout.text: Ideal when users edit things for a while — a document, a profile, a cart. Holding a lock for minutes would block everyone.

changes: ~ Ben’s write rejected (version changed) → retries → sold out

steps.title: Isolation levels
body: Databases offer several isolation levels. Stronger ones prevent more anomalies, but make transactions wait or abort more often.

PreventsCost
Read committedDirty readsLowest
Snapshot / repeatable read+ changing reads; lost updates in some databases1Some aborts
SerializableEverything: as if one at a timeMost aborts — retry
<small><sup>1</sup> PostgreSQL aborts the second writer; MySQL’s repeatable read lets the lost update through. Same name, different guarantees — check your database’s documentation.</small>

callout.text: With serializable, the database may abort a transaction rather than allow an anomaly. Your code must catch that and retry.

steps.title: Case: locking a row that doesn’t exist yet
body: A new booking flow drops the seat counter and checks the bookings table instead: “is there a booking for seat 7? No — insert one.” Both transactions even use FOR UPDATE…

…but there is no row to lock yet. Both see nothing, both insert, and seat 7 is booked twice. A row that appears between your check and your write is a phantom; deciding on what you read and then writing something else is called write skew.

callout.text: Fixes: serializable isolation, locking an existing parent row (the seat itself), or a unique constraint — see the next steps.

changes: − FOR UPDATE finds no row to lock

steps.title: Case: the deadlock
body: Locks bring their own trap. Ana transfers money from account A to B: she locks A, then asks for B. At the same instant Ben transfers from B to A: he locks B, then asks for A.
Each waits for the other, forever. The database detects the cycle — immediately in some engines, after about a second in others — and aborts one transaction (Ben’s), which must retry.

callout.text: Prevent it by always taking locks in the same order — for example, lowest account id first. Then a cycle can’t form.

changes: + Two transfers lock A and B in opposite orders

tags.text: Ana holds A · waits for B
Ben holds B · waits for A

card.title: A wait cycle
lines: Ana: lock A … waiting for B
Ben: lock B … waiting for A
= fix: always lock lowest id first

steps.title: Constraints: the last line of defence
body: Code changes, and someone will eventually write a booking path that forgets the lock. So let the database enforce the rule itself: a unique constraint on (concert, seat) in the bookings table.
Now a second booking for seat 7 is rejected with a duplicate-key error, whatever the application code does.

callout.text: Encode invariants as constraints — unique, foreign key, check (balance ≥ 0). They hold even when the code has bugs.

steps.title: Case: a lock held during a payment
body: To be safe, someone moves the card payment inside the booking transaction: lock seat 7, call the payment provider, then commit. The provider takes 3 seconds.
For those 3 seconds the seat stays locked, and every other buyer of it waits — each holding a database connection. On sale day the connection pool runs dry and the whole site stalls.

callout.text: Never wait on anything slow — a user, a payment API, an email — while holding a database lock or an open transaction.

changes: ~ Seat 7 locked for 3 s per attempt

steps.title: Reserve, pay, then confirm
body: Split it into short steps. Transaction 1 marks seat 7 as held for Ana until 12:10 and commits at once. Then she pays — outside any transaction. Transaction 2 marks the seat sold.
If she never pays, a cleanup job releases holds that have expired. Ben is told immediately that the seat is taken — no waiting, no locks held for seconds.

callout.text: This is the “seat held for 10 minutes” timer on every ticket and airline site. A reservation with an expiry replaces a long lock.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Read-then-write under concurrency causes races and lost updates.
  • Fix with row locks, a single atomic UPDATE, or version checks.
  • Isolation levels trade correctness for waiting and retries.
  • Lock in a consistent order; back rules with constraints.
  • Keep transactions short: hold a reservation, never a lock, while waiting on payments.
